coachingPoints: Drop the foot, not the ball — the ball stays high while your foot does the work.
The drop step should land you at the rim, not 2 meters away — start close.
Keep the ball high through the step; dropping it invites strips.
Power up off two feet when possible — more balance, more fouls drawn.
Read the defender's chest: if they lean middle, drop baseline; if they lean baseline, drop middle.
commonMistakes: Dropping the foot but leaving the ball low — strip city.
Taking the drop step too far from the basket — now you're under the rim with no angle.
Leading with the shoulder into the defender — that's a charge; step around them, not through them.
Telegraphing it with a big wind-up — the drop step should be one quick, quiet step.
description: The baseline power move: one drop step past the defender's hip and you're at the rim.
gameSituations: Catching on the low block with the defender on your high side — drop baseline.
Against a defender who overplays the middle — the baseline is wide open.
Late-clock post touches — one move, no wasted dribbles.

howTo.detail: Catch the ball on the block with your back to the basket, defender on your back. Chin the ball and feel where their weight is — usually leaning toward the middle.
howTo.title: Catch and feel the defender

howTo.detail: Swing your baseline-side foot (the foot nearer the baseline) in a big step toward the baseline, landing between the defender and the basket. Your body now seals them behind you.
howTo.title: Drop step to the baseline

howTo.detail: Dribble once, hard, as you step — one power dribble is all you need. Keep the ball on your outside hip, away from the defender's reach.
howTo.title: One power dribble

howTo.detail: Gather off the dribble and power up on two feet, extending the ball-side arm to the rim. Finish with the board or straight up, through any contact.
howTo.title: Power up and finish

title: Drop Step
whatIsIt: The drop step is the fundamental post power move: from a back-to-the-basket catch, you swing one foot toward the baseline (or middle), stepping past the defender's hip and sealing them behind you on the way to the rim.
It's called a 'drop' because your foot drops into the lane like an anchor. One step, one dribble, one finish — no wasted motion. Every great post scorer's game starts here.
whyItMatters: The drop step is the highest-percentage post move because it ends at the rim with the defender sealed. Defenses have to send help to stop it, which opens up kick-outs. If you can drop step both directions, you're a scoring threat on every touch.
